lead: Open thin-walled columns such as channels, angles and Z-sections are stiff in bending but very weak in torsion, and for most of them the centroid C and the shear centre S are at different points. An axial load through C then makes bending and twisting grow together once the column starts to deflect, and the column buckles in a combined bending and twisting mode at a load below its Euler load. Stringers and frames are open sections, so this check decides their length between supports.
prereq: You need: Euler column buckling, the shear centre of a channel and the torsion constant J = Σbt³/3 of open sections, and the crippling stress from local buckling and crippling.

sections.h3: Why an open column twists as it buckles

blocks.text: An open section resists torque mainly through its tiny St Venant constant J = Σbt³/3, plus resistance to warping when its ends or neighbours stop the section warping freely. That second effect is measured by the warping constant C<sub>w</sub> (mm⁶). The shear centre S is the point a transverse load must pass through to cause no twist.

Let x₀ and y₀ locate S from the centroid C. While the column is straight, an axial load P through C has no moment about the column axis. Once the column deflects by u and v and twists by θ, the section rotates about S, which moves C sideways by an amount proportional to θ and the offset. The axial load, now acting along a curved line through the displaced centroids, produces a twisting moment about S of order P(x₀ v″ − y₀ u″) per unit length, and the twist in turn adds to the bending. The two grow together: flexural–torsional buckling.

When C and S coincide, as in an I-section or a cruciform, the coupling vanishes: the column buckles either by bending about one axis at the Euler load, or by pure twisting about its axis, the torsional instability that short cruciforms show. A singly symmetric section has S on its axis of symmetry; bending about that axis couples with twist, while bending in the plane of symmetry stays a separate Euler mode.
For a pin-ended column free to warp at its ends, three uncoupled loads are defined:
P<sub>x</sub> = π²E I<sub>x</sub>/L²,   P<sub>y</sub> = π²E I<sub>y</sub>/L²,   P<sub>t</sub> = (GJ + π²E C<sub>w</sub>/L²)/r₀²,   r₀² = (I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub>)/A + x₀² + y₀²
blocks.where: P<sub>x</sub>, P<sub>y</sub> are the Euler loads for bending about the centroidal x and y axes (N); P<sub>t</sub> the torsional buckling load (N); I<sub>x</sub>, I<sub>y</sub> the centroidal second moments (mm⁴); A the area (mm²); G the shear modulus (N/mm²); J the torsion constant (mm⁴); C<sub>w</sub> the warping constant (mm⁶); L the length (mm); r₀ the polar radius of gyration about the shear centre (mm).

blocks.text: GJ is St Venant's resistance and π²EC<sub>w</sub>/L² the warping resistance; the second fades as L grows. In general the buckling load is the smallest root of the cubic:
r₀²(P − P<sub>x</sub>)(P − P<sub>y</sub>)(P − P<sub>t</sub>) − P²x₀²(P − P<sub>y</sub>) − P²y₀²(P − P<sub>x</sub>) = 0
blocks.where: x₀, y₀ are the coordinates of the shear centre from the centroid (mm). The x₀ offset couples twist with bending about x, and y₀ with bending about y.

blocks.text: For a section symmetric about x (y₀ = 0) the cubic splits: P = P<sub>y</sub> is a pure Euler mode, and bending about x couples with twist through (P<sub>x</sub> − P)(P<sub>t</sub> − P) − P²x₀²/r₀² = 0. The smaller root of this quadratic is always below both P<sub>x</sub> and P<sub>t</sub>, so the column is weaker than either mode alone suggests. A closed tube has J hundreds of times larger, so P<sub>t</sub> is far above the Euler loads and flexural–torsional buckling hardly ever governs.

Euler's formula σ = π²E/(L/ρ)² holds for slender columns, with ρ = √(I/A) the radius of gyration. A short thin-walled column cannot reach Euler's stress: it cripples first, at σ<sub>cs</sub>. Between the two, local buckling and bending interact, and a parabola due to Johnson joins them:

blocks.where: σ<sub>c</sub> is the column failing stress (N/mm²); σ<sub>cs</sub> the crippling stress (N/mm²); L′ the effective length (mm), equal to L for pinned ends; ρ the least radius of gyration (mm).

blocks.text: The parabola starts at σ<sub>cs</sub> for a stub and touches the Euler curve at σ = σ<sub>cs</sub>/2, where L′/ρ = √(2π²E/σ<sub>cs</sub>). Above that slenderness use Euler; below it use the parabola. For open sections, also check the flexural–torsional load, which can be lower than both.

examples.question: A pin-ended channel column 800 mm long has a web of 60 mm and two flanges of 30 mm (mid-line), all 2 mm thick, with E = 70 GPa and G = 27 GPa. The channel is symmetric about the horizontal x axis. Find the Euler loads, the torsional load and the flexural–torsional buckling load, and say which mode governs.
steps: Area and centroid: A = 2 × (60 + 2 × 30) = 240 mm²; x̄ = b²t/A = 7.5 mm from the web, towards the flanges.
Shear centre: e = 3b²/(h + 6b) = 2700/240 = 11.25 mm outside the web, so x₀ = 7.5 + 11.25 = 18.75 mm from C, and y₀ = 0.
Second moments: I<sub>x</sub> = t h³/12 + 2bt(h/2)² = 36,000 + 108,000 = 144,000 mm⁴; I<sub>y</sub> = h t x̄² + 2[t b³/12 + b t(b/2 − x̄)²] = 22,500 mm⁴.
Torsion: J = t³(h + 2b)/3 = 320 mm⁴; C<sub>w</sub> = t b³h²(3b + 2h)/[12(6b + h)] = 1.417 × 10⁷ mm⁶.

Coupled mode (x with twist): x₀²/r₀² = 0.3363. (P<sub>x</sub> − P)(P<sub>t</sub> − P) − 0.3363P² = 0 becomes 0.6637P² − 178,350P + 3.560 × 10⁹ = 0, whose smaller root is P = 21,718 N. Substituting back leaves a residual of 1.1e-06 N², so the root is right.
Comparison: P<sub>y</sub> = 24.3 kN, P<sub>t</sub> = 22.9 kN, flexural–torsional 21.7 kN. The flexural–torsional mode governs, 11% below the lower Euler load.
examples.answer: P<sub>x</sub> = 155.4 kN, P<sub>y</sub> = 24.3 kN, P<sub>t</sub> = 22.9 kN; the column buckles by bending and twisting together at 21.7 kN.

examples.question: The formed channel of the crippling chapter (web 60 mm, flanges 25 mm, 1.5 mm thick, A = 165 mm², σ<sub>cs</sub> = 179.4 MPa, E = 72 GPa) is used as a pin-ended column 500 mm long. Find its column failing stress by the Johnson parabola, using the least radius of gyration.
steps: Least second moment, about the axis parallel to the web (mid-line dimensions): I<sub>y</sub> = 10,298 mm⁴ for the mid-line area 165 mm².
Tangent point: √(2π²E/σ<sub>cs</sub>) = √(2π² × 72,000/179.4) = 89.0. Since 63.3 < 89.0, the parabola applies.

Check: Euler alone would give π² × 72,000/63.3² = 177 MPa, almost the stub crippling stress. At this middling slenderness local buckling and bending interact, and the parabola gives the lower, realistic 134 MPa.
Failing load: 134.0 × 165 = 22,118 N. A flexural–torsional check, as in the first example, should follow.
examples.answer: L′/ρ = 63.3; σ<sub>c</sub> = 134 MPa and the column fails at about 22.1 kN.

traps: Saying an axial load through C applies a torque P × offset to a straight column. The twisting moment appears only after the column bends.
Leaving out C<sub>w</sub> for a short open column. J is tiny, so warping resistance often supplies most of P<sub>t</sub>.
Measuring r₀ about the centroid. r₀² includes x₀² + y₀², the offset of the shear centre.
Taking the smallest of P<sub>x</sub>, P<sub>y</sub> and P<sub>t</sub> as the answer for a channel. The coupled root is below the modes it combines.
Using Euler's formula for a short thin-walled column. Below L′/ρ = √(2π²E/σ<sub>cs</sub>) the column fails by the Johnson parabola, starting from σ<sub>cs</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the torsional buckling load of a pin-ended column and define r₀.
quiz.a: P<sub>t</sub> = (GJ + π²EC<sub>w</sub>/L²)/r₀², with r₀² = (I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub>)/A + x₀² + y₀², the polar radius of gyration about the shear centre squared.

quiz.q: Why does an axial load through the centroid twist an open channel column, but not a straight one?
quiz.a: While straight, the load is parallel to the axis and has no moment about it. Once the column bends and twists, the section rotates about S and the load acts along a curved line through the displaced centroids, offset from S; that gives a twisting moment growing with the deflection.

quiz.q: A section has A = 300 mm², I<sub>x</sub> + I<sub>y</sub> = 480,000 mm⁴ and y₀ = 10 mm. Find r₀².
For the channel of the first example, find P<sub>t</sub> if the column were twice as long.
quiz.a: π²EC<sub>w</sub>/L² falls to a quarter: 3,825,436 N·mm². P<sub>t</sub> = (8,640,000 + 3,825,436)/1045.3 = 11,925 N.

quiz.q: Explain why a closed tube rarely fails by flexural–torsional buckling, while an open channel of the same material and area often does.
quiz.a: The tube's J = 4A²/∮ds/t is hundreds of times the open value Σbt³/3, so P<sub>t</sub> is far above the Euler loads; and for a symmetric tube S coincides with C, so there is no coupling. The channel has a small J and an offset shear centre.

quiz.q: For a column symmetric about x, show that the coupled root lies below both P<sub>x</sub> and P<sub>t</sub>.
quiz.a: f(P) = (P<sub>x</sub> − P)(P<sub>t</sub> − P) − P²x₀²/r₀². At P = 0, f = P<sub>x</sub>P<sub>t</sub> > 0. At P = min(P<sub>x</sub>, P<sub>t</sub>) the product is zero and f = −P²x₀²/r₀² < 0. So f changes sign between 0 and the smaller of the two, and the root lies there.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design codes for cold-formed steel and aluminium members contain the same cubic. Search for flexural–torsional buckling and warping constant.
